carpenter.intro: Learn carpentry from measurement to finished structure. Build furniture, frames, and fittings with precision — a trade with constant demand across West Africa.

skills.name: Measuring
skills.description: Get every number right the first time.

modules.title: Measure twice, cut once
modules.content:
This is not a saying. It's a rule that saves material and time.

Tools

  • Tape measure — the standard. 5m minimum.
  • Steel rule — for precision marking on small work
  • Try square — for 90° angles
  • Combination square — for 45° and 90° plus depth marking
  • Marking gauge — for parallel lines
  • Pencil — sharp. Always sharp.

Rules

  1. Measure from the same reference point every time
  2. Write numbers down immediately
  3. Double-check before cutting
  4. Mark the waste side of the line

steps.q: You need a board 47.3cm long. Your tape has mm marks. Where do you mark?
You cut a board and it's 3mm short. What do you do?
o: Cut a new piece and check your measurement technique
steps.f: Recut and figure out where the error came from.

steps.q: You must mark a line parallel to the edge, 5cm in. Which tool?
steps.f: A marking gauge cuts a consistent parallel line.

skillDomains.name: Cutting & Joining
skillDomains.description: The core skills — cutting accurately and joining strongly.

skills.name: Sawing
skills.description: Cut straight, cut square, cut clean.

modules.title: The right saw for the job
modules.content:
Hand saws

  • Crosscut saw — cuts across the grain
  • Rip saw — cuts along the grain
  • Tenon saw — fine teeth for joinery

Power saws

  • Circular saw — fast, straight cuts
  • Jigsaw — curves and cutouts
  • Mitre saw — accurate angled cuts

Technique

  1. Mark the cut line on the waste side
  2. Start the cut with a few back strokes
  3. Keep the saw at the correct angle
  4. Let the saw do the work
  5. Support the offcut

steps.q: You need a clean cut across a 5cm thick plank. Which saw?
steps.f: Crosscut for cutting across the grain.

steps.q: The offcut splinters at the end of every cut. How do you fix this?
o: Support the offcut or score the line first
steps.f: Splintering happens when the wood is unsupported.

steps.q: Your cut wanders off the line. Most common cause?
o: Forcing the saw or starting at the wrong angle

skills.name: Joinery
skills.description: The joints that hold a piece of furniture together for decades.

modules.title: Common wood joints
modules.content:
Butt joint

Two pieces joined end to end. Weak without reinforcement.

Dado / housing joint

A groove cut across the grain of one piece to receive the end of another.

Mortise and tenon

A projecting tenon fits into a cut mortise. Very strong.

Dovetail

Interlocking angled joint. Extremely strong.

Half-lap

Two pieces overlap halfway. Used for frames.

steps.q: You're building a bookshelf. Which joint for attaching the shelves to the sides?
steps.f: Dado joints support the shelf along its whole edge.

steps.q: You're building a chair. Which joint for the legs?
steps.f: Chairs take heavy stress. Mortise and tenon is strongest.

steps.q: You're building a drawer. Which joint for the sides?
steps.f: Dovetails resist pulling apart and look professional.

modules.title: Build a joint sample board
modules.prompt: Create at least 5 wood joint samples: butt with dowels, dado, half-lap, mortise and tenon, and dovetail. Mount them on a board with labels.
steps: Label with joint name and where it's used

skillDomains.name: Installation
skillDomains.description: Fit finished work into buildings — doors, windows, cabinets.

modules.title: Hanging a door
modules.content:
The process

  1. Measure the opening precisely
  2. Cut the door with correct clearances (3mm sides, 5mm top, 8-10mm bottom)
  3. Mark hinge positions on frame and door
  4. Cut hinge recesses with a chisel
  5. Fit hinges to frame, then hang the door
  6. Mark the lock position
  7. Fit lock, handle, and latch
  8. Test swing and latch operation

Common mistakes

  • Clearance too tight — door sticks in humid weather
  • Hinges not aligned — door swings on its own
  • Lock too close to edge — wood splits

steps.q: How much clearance should a door have at the sides?
steps.f: 3mm per side allows the door to swing freely.

steps.q: The installed door swings open on its own when released. What's wrong?
steps.f: Self-swinging doors mean hinges are not on the same plane.

steps.q: The bottom of the door rubs on the floor. What do you do?

modules.title: Fitting cabinets and wardrobes
modules.content:
Level and plumb are everything

Before installing anything, verify the walls are level and plumb. Most walls are not perfect.

Order of installation

  1. Mark the level line at the top of the cabinet run
  2. Fix wall brackets or a hanging rail
  3. Hang the first cabinet — the level one
  4. Attach subsequent cabinets to the first
  5. Level the run as a whole before fixing to the wall
  6. Add the worktop or shelf
  7. Add doors, drawers, and handles

skillDomains.name: Finishing & Client Work
skillDomains.description: The final touches and the business side.

modules.title: The finishing process
modules.content:
Sanding

Start with coarse grit (80-120) to remove marks. Work up to fine (180-220). Finish with 320+ for furniture-grade.

Types of finish

  • Varnish — durable, glossy or matte
  • Oil — penetrates, natural look
  • Wax — traditional, low protection
  • Lacquer — spray-applied
  • Paint — opaque, durable

Rules

  • Sanding between coats
  • Wipe dust with tack cloth
  • Thin coats, not thick ones
  • Don't rush drying times

steps.q: A client wants a matte, natural look they can reapply themselves. Which finish?
steps.f: Oil gives natural look and can be reapplied easily.

steps.q: You're finishing a kitchen table. Which finish?
steps.f: Multiple coats of varnish give the best protection.

steps.q: You see brush marks in the finish after drying. What caused this?
o: Too thick a coat, or brushing after it started setting
steps.f: Brush marks come from thick coats or brushing too long.

modules.title: Pricing carpentry work
modules.content:
Four-part price

  1. Materials — timber, hardware, finish
  2. Labour — hours × your rate
  3. Overhead — workshop, tools, transport
  4. Margin — 30-50% for custom furniture

The rule

Never quote a custom piece without seeing the space.

modules.title: Quote a custom wardrobe
modules.prompt: A client wants a built-in wardrobe: 2.4m wide, 2.2m tall, 0.6m deep. Materials: timber 400,000 Le, hardware 80,000 Le, finish 40,000 Le. Labour: 5 days at 30,000 Le/day. Overhead: 60,000 Le. Margin: 35%. Calculate the quote.
modules.context: Custom furniture is the highest-value carpentry work.
